source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Eye-tracking replication of the chess Einstellung effect with a new design: choose-a-move, one problem that holds both a familiar move and a better move.
numbers: 34 players: 17 experts (mean CFC 2223, range 1876-2580) and 17 unrated club novices. 4 experimental problems plus 8 fillers each, 3 minute cap, EyeLink 1000 at 1000 Hz.
limits: Small N. Only 4 problems. Novices were unrated, so the skill scale is coarse.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as our agent: first solution found fast, then search that looks like checking but stays near the first idea.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: With a good-but-suboptimal familiar move (Problem 1), experts were no better than novices at avoiding it.
numbers: 8 of 17 experts AND 8 of 17 novices chose the Einstellung move (Ba7) over the optimal move. Overall experts still scored higher on move quality (t(32)=6.04, p<.001).
limits: One problem carries this result. Expertise helped overall but not on the trap item.
agent_relevance: Skill does not protect against a good-enough first answer. A stronger model is not a fix by itself; needs a signal that forces a second look.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Eye movements split by outcome. Players who chose the familiar move kept looking at its region the whole trial. Experts who found the optimal move gradually looked away.
numbers: Optimal-move experts (n=9): linear trend F(1,34)=43.45, p<.001. Experts who chose the familiar move (n=8): no trend F<1. Novices who chose it (n=8): F(1,30)=1.76, p=.194.
quote: Having found one solution, expert chess players reported that they were looking for a better one.
limits: Looking is correlational with choice. Groups formed after the fact by their choice.
agent_relevance: A detector for 'still attending to the first answer's features' is a possible impasse signal. For an LLM the analogue is tokens that re-argue the first answer.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Boundary condition: when the familiar move was a blunder (clear loss), the effect nearly vanished for everyone.
numbers: Problems 2-4 (blunders): all 17 experts and most novices avoided the familiar move. Looking time fell over the trial for experts F(1,66)=79.88, p<.001 and novices F(1,66)=10.84, p<.01.
quote: Thus, the Einstellung effect may be especially pernicious when problem-solvers are not given feedback that they are using a suboptimal strategy
limits: Authors propose a feedback account (the blunder tells the player the idea fails). Not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G3: a real failing output breaks the fixation. A silent 'good enough' answer does not. Matches 'revise only from real output'.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Familiar pattern is seen very fast, and experts get there sooner.
numbers: Time to first fixation on the trap region: experts 407 ms, novices 719 ms (t(32)=2.99, p<.01). Total dwell time and percent looking time (0.62 vs 0.63) did not differ by expertise.
limits: Only the first move of the process. Interview recall is retrospective.
agent_relevance: The first schema is cheap and instant for experts. The cost shows up later, in whether it is dropped.

source: Sheridan & Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Retrospective interviews: some players never ruled out the false mate.
numbers: Among 8 experts and 8 novices who chose the suboptimal move, 2 experts and 4 novices did not rule out checkmate. The 9 optimal-move experts all said they ruled out the mate first, then searched the other side of the board.
quote: I didn't see the mate on a7, so I looked at the other side of the board
limits: Self-report, after the fact. Small counts.
agent_relevance: The successful route was an explicit 'rule out the familiar pattern, then search elsewhere' step. Candidate for an operator at S6.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
finding: Original eye-tracking study. Candidate Masters who found the familiar 5-move mate said they were looking for something shorter, but kept looking at the squares of the familiar solution.
numbers: Looking at familiar-mate squares vs optimal squares across 6 time periods: no change for the 2-solution problem (F(5,20)=0.6, ns). Control group on the 1-solution problem shifted toward optimal squares (F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta squared .75). Players who were blocked took 37 s to settle on the long mate.
quote: Having found one solution, expert chess players reported that they were looking for a better one.
limits: Very small groups (about 5 per group, t(8) in the paper). Eye tracker at 50 Hz. One position pair.
agent_relevance: Verbal reports of 'I am searching' are not evidence of search. Fits G10: reasoning text is not evidence.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
finding: Blocked players could still solve the easy version, so the problem itself was not too hard. Lingering cost on that second problem.
numbers: 1-solution problem: control group 79 s (SD 25), all solved. Blocked group solved it in 148 s (SD 90) after failing the 2-solution problem; difference t(8)=1.67, p=.13, d=1.2 (not significant alone).
limits: Underpowered in Exp 1. Luchins' original total block was not reproduced: all experts found the 3-move mate once the trap was gone.
agent_relevance: Even after the trap is removed, a prior wrong frame slows work. Fresh context per attempt (S3) removes this carry-over.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
finding: Experiment 2 tested the carry-over with a larger sample across skill levels.
numbers: Fresh players on the 1-solution problem found the mate in about half the time of players who had first met the 2-solution problem: t(44)=2.16, p=.036, d=.65. Interaction with skill (IM, Master, Candidate Master) not significant, F(2,40)=0.9, p>.40.
quote: Like a decaying priming effect, it continued to distract the players.
limits: Between-subject comparison against an earlier sample from the same lab. Effect is modest (p=.036).
agent_relevance: Effect size d=.65 for carry-over of a wrong frame supports isolating attempts.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
finding: Headline size: the familiar solution cut expert performance to that of players about three standard deviations lower in skill.
numbers: Reported as 'three standard deviations' lower; described in the opened Sheridan & Reingold 2013 and Bilalic et al. 2008 texts from the earlier Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet 2008 Cognitive Psychology paper (not opened here).
limits: Number quoted from secondary descriptions. The Cognitive Psychology paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Expertise does not remove the effect, but it also does not equal the weak players' ceiling once the trap is removed.

source: Ellis & Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements
finding: Einstellung also appears in a simple anagram task in ordinary participants, with eye data that show both interference and help from familiarity.
numbers: 60 participants. 52.7% correct, 4.2% wrong, 43.1% timed out. Correct trials: 15.3 s (familiar word centre) vs 13.4 s (nonword) t(59)=3.25, p<.01. Accuracy 51.7% vs 53.8%, not significant.
limits: Not experts. Cost shows in speed more than accuracy. Familiar word also sped first look: 'facilitation' at one stage and 'interference' at another.
agent_relevance: Familiarity both speeds encoding and hurts integration. A fixation cost may be seen in latency or token count before it shows in accuracy.

source: Ellis & Reingold (2014) The Einstellung effect in anagram problem solving: evidence from eye movements
finding: Familiar word trials caused more re-checking of both the word and the loose letters.
numbers: Dwells on central string 8.11 (word) vs 6.76 (nonword) t(59)=4.69; dwells on single letters 10.45 vs 8.53 t(59)=4.80, both p<.001. Effect same for solutions that felt sudden (69%) and gradual (31%).
limits: Eye analyses only on correct trials.
agent_relevance: Cost of the familiar unit is a difficulty combining pieces, not simply missing information.

source: Semantic accessibility is associated with reduced experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving (2026, Chinese Remote Associates Task)
finding: Newer test of the knowledge-helps versus knowledge-hurts question: strong induced strategy hurt only when semantic access was low.
numbers: 30 participants, 2x2 within-subject. Interaction F(1,29)=4.88, p=.035, partial eta squared .14. Low accessibility: strong 0.70 vs weak 1.27 correct, p=.009, d=.52. High accessibility: 2.07 vs 1.90, p=.538, d=.12. Main effect of accessibility F(1,29)=24.86, p<.001.
limits: Single lab, N=30, interaction p=.035, Chinese-language task, not yet replicated. Main effect of induction itself was not significant (F=1.40).
agent_relevance: Having many alternative links available (broad retrieval) may buffer fixation. For an agent: widen candidate generation before committing.

source: Semantic accessibility is associated with reduced experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving (2026, Chinese Remote Associates Task)
finding: A matched-item check suggests induction cost is real in the low-access condition and not in the high-access condition.
numbers: Matched pairs n=15. Low accessibility: weak induction cost 0.122 (d=.89, p=.004), strong 0.072 (d=.73, p=.013). High accessibility: 0.072 (d=.45, p=.103), 0.067 (d=.45, p=.104).
limits: Cost sizes for high access are similar in size to low; they just fail significance with n=15. Reading this as 'buffer' is shaky.
agent_relevance: Treat as a hint. Do not build a rule on it.

source: Campitelli, Connors, Bilalic & Hambrick (2015) Psychological perspectives on expertise (Frontiers editorial, 35 articles)
finding: Editorial for a 35-article issue; flags eye-movement work on the Einstellung effect as relevant to expert flexibility.
numbers: 35 articles in chess, music, perception, teaching, ICU diagnosis, sports, mathematics and more. Four used eye movements. Ellis & Reingold 2014 is the Einstellung entry.
limits: Editorial summary, not data.
agent_relevance: Shows that the Einstellung line sits inside broader expertise work; no single study settles flexibility.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Deliberate practice explains a modest share of skill differences, much less outside games and music.
numbers: 157 effect sizes, 11,135 participants. Variance explained by practice: games 26%, music 21%, sports 18%, education 4%, professions under 1%. Larger for predictable activities than for unpredictable ones.
limits: Practice hours were self-reported in most studies (96 of 157 used questionnaires). Critics (Ericsson) say many activities were not true deliberate practice.
agent_relevance: Practice volume alone does not buy adaptability. In unpredictable domains, practice predicts little. A scaffold should not assume more repetition fixes rigid choices.

source: Burgoyne, Nye, Macnamara, Charness & Hambrick (2019) The impact of domain-specific experience on chess skill: reanalysis of a key study
finding: Chess reanalysis: training plus experience accounted for most, not all, of rating variance.
numbers: SEM on Charness et al. (2005) data: serious chess activity and formal instruction (latent) plus starting age explained 63% of variance in peak rating. Starting age beta=-.15. The claim that formal instruction boosts the effect of serious study was not supported. Earlier Hambrick et al. 2014: 34% of chess variance, 30% of music.
limits: One data set. Self-reported histories. Different estimates (34% vs 63%) show the answer depends on the model.
agent_relevance: Estimates of how much practice matters swing a lot with method. Be wary of any single figure.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (mARC-QA)
finding: mARC-QA: 100 hand-written medical questions that put a familiar cue next to a blocker, to trigger Einstellung in LLMs. Most models failed.
numbers: Physicians (5, mean) 66% (SE 5.3). Best: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini 1.5 pro 50%, o1 48%. Many models under 50%, some near chance (<20%), medical fine-tunes near 0%. 15 runs per model, chain of thought used, temperature 0.
limits: Only 100 items, written by the authors. 5 physicians, 2 hour limit. Models from Dec 2024.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the topic. Plain models fall for the familiar pattern even when logic blocks it.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (mARC-QA)
finding: Overconfidence and the human-miss set.
numbers: Items missed by physician majority: 20 of 100; humans 36% on them vs 73% on the rest. DeepSeek-R1: confidently correct on 45%, confidently incorrect on 40%, indeterminate 15%. Larger models better calibrated yet still overconfident. Llama 405b scored below 70b.
limits: Odd Llama result may be quantisation (authors' guess). Confidence from sample consistency.
agent_relevance: Agreement across samples is not proof (G4). Confident wrong answers on trap items are common.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility in clinical problem-solving
finding: Follow-up: reasoning models closed the gap on mARC.
numbers: Best: Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763). No significant difference from physicians (0.66, CI 0.55-0.75) for Claude 4.1 Opus, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1, Grok-4-Fast-Reasoning. Highest reasoning effort was used. Reasoning variants beat non-reasoning counterparts.
limits: Preprint. Same 100 items, same authors, only 5 physicians so the human CI is wide. Items may have leaked into training.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode helps against a familiar-cue trap. Supports allowing thinking when a conflict between cue and blocker is detected.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM reasoning enable flexibility in clinical problem-solving
finding: On items physicians most often missed, top models beat humans.
numbers: Human-miss set: 20 of 100 items, human 36%. Claude 4.1 Opus decisively correct on 55.0%, decisively wrong on 25.0%, indeterminate 20.0%. Top five models: 55% to 70% correct with high confidence.
limits: Small set (20 items), wide intervals (e.g. 39.9-80.0).
agent_relevance: Models and humans fail on different items. Combining views (human or model) may help; still a hint.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set?
finding: Mental-set test on LLMs using math equivalence problems (from DeCaro 2016). Weak evidence; results are mixed.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, GPT-4o. Six problems per condition. Few-shot exact match: GPT-4o shortcut 0.33, shortcut after complex 0.66, complex 0.66, complex then shortcut 0.83; Llama-8B 0.16 or 0. With CoT: GPT-4o 0.66 / 0.66 / 0.83 / 0.83. Steps per solved problem: 3 under CoT.
limits: Six items per cell, no statistics, accuracy in steps of 0.16. The 'more steps means mental set' reading is not tested against a control. Shortcut problems were not solved better after shortcut practice.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as proof that LLMs show Einstellung. Chain of thought changed strategy length, not flexibility.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large language models are fixated by red herrings (Only Connect Wall dataset)
finding: Only Connect Wall: puzzles with built-in red herrings. Models stay far below humans; removing red herrings raises scores sharply.
numbers: Humans solved 285 of 494 walls and 1405 of 1976 groups. GPT-4 (best) solved 7 walls (5-shot) and 269 groups; GPT-3.5-turbo 2 walls, 149 groups. Without cross-wall decoys (OCW-Randomized) GPT-4 5-shot: 68 walls, 655 groups. With decoys removed via WordNet: 298 to 471 walls, 1926 groups at 0-shot. More shots did not help.
limits: Randomizing groups also changes difficulty, so the drop cannot be assigned to decoys alone. GPT-4-0314 and GPT-3.5 only. No open model results.
agent_relevance: Decoys that look like the answer hurt LLMs. Tests of an operator that sets aside the obvious grouping have a ready benchmark.

source: Fenwick, Campitelli & Thompson (2026) Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise
finding: 2026 theory paper links Gigerenzer's adaptive toolbox to expertise: tools are learned, automatised and selected by experience.
numbers: Heuristic defined as ignoring part of the information; has a search rule, a stopping rule, a decision rule. Probability-format Bayesian accuracy can be as low as 4%; natural-frequency formats typically 20-50% (McDowell & Jacobs 2017).
quote: a strategy that ignores part of the information in order to make decisions more quickly, frugally, and with little loss in accuracy
limits: Theory and review, no new data. Argues a consistent minority succeed without scaffolds.
agent_relevance: S6 operator choice: pick a tool by the structure of the problem, and learn which tool fit which task.

source: Fenwick, Campitelli & Thompson (2026) Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise
finding: Training evidence summarised: representation training beat rule training and lasted longer.
numbers: Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer 2001, as described here: baseline near 0; after training about 60% (rules) vs 75-90% (frequency representations); after 5 weeks rule training fell to about 20%, frequency training stayed high; with a reward rule-trained people held about 70%.
limits: Secondary description. Original 2001 paper not opened. Reward effect points to practice not format.
agent_relevance: Which representation the tool starts from matters more than adding instruction. Tool choice can be taught.

source: Fenwick, Campitelli & Thompson (2026) Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise
finding: Fast-and-frugal trees work in medicine partly because they copy clinicians' existing cue structure (Marewski & Gigerenzer 2012).
numbers: No new numbers. Claim: heuristic success depends on a match between the tool and cue structure in the environment (ecological rationality).
limits: Argument, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Tool selection should be conditioned on cue structure, not a global rule. Supports spend-by-difficulty (G12).

source: Siebert et al. (2025) Fast-and-frugal trees to inform intervention decisions in elite athletes (PLOS ONE)
finding: Fast-and-frugal trees built from athlete diagnostics can predict which training intervention to use.
numbers: 466 German elite athletes, six cues from PCA. Trampoline tree (4 cues): 90% correct. Volleyball tree (4 cues): 75% correct. Test on 40% held-out subsample.
limits: Not a study of reflection in athletes; it is about simple decision rules. Small subsamples per sport.
agent_relevance: Simple one-reason decision trees can reach decent accuracy in a narrow domain. Low evidence for general transfer.

source: Planning, cognitive reflection, inter-temporal choice, and risky choice in chess players (2025)
finding: Chess players beat non-players on planning and cognitive reflection; risk choice difference unclear.
numbers: 25 chess players vs 25 non-chess players. Better on Tower of London and Cognitive Reflection Test. Prefer later rewards. Risky choice: evidence for a difference very weak (Bayes factors).
limits: Cross-sectional, no causality. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Experts in a rule-bound domain may show more reflective responding in general, but this may be selection. Not evidence that reflection transfers.

source: Luchins (1942) Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung
finding: Original water-jug demonstration: five introductory problems with one method, then a problem needing a new method.
numbers: As described in Sheridan & Reingold 2013: many participants said the extinction problem was insoluble; control group without the introductory problems solved it. Exact counts not read.
limits: Not opened. Numbers not verified here.
agent_relevance: Founding result for the repeated-success-then-trap design.

source: Binz & Schulz (2022) Reconstructing the Einstellung effect (Computational Brain & Behavior)
finding: A resource-rational model reproduces Luchins' original results, so the effect may be an efficient trade-off, not just a failure.
numbers: From a web summary only: three principles (prefer simple solutions, avoid costly computation, adapt to problem statistics); an ablation found all three needed to reproduce Luchins' thesis data.
limits: Not opened. Summary secondhand.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation: persisting with a cheap known method can be rational. The scaffold should switch only on a signal (G1), not always.

source: Blech, Gaschler & Bilalic (2020) Why do people fail to see simple solutions? Think-aloud protocols and the Einstellung effect
finding: Think-aloud study on water jugs: people who showed the effect kept trying variations of the earlier successful method.
numbers: From a search snippet only. No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as the chess eye data from a different method.

source: Hatano & Inagaki (1986) Two courses of expertise
finding: Origin of the routine versus adaptive expertise distinction: routine experts are fast at familiar tasks; adaptive experts also vary and invent procedures.
numbers: Not opened this session. No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Cited from background knowledge only.
agent_relevance: Names the goal: fast on familiar items, flexible on new ones. Our scaffold aims at both.
